questions.knowledge_point: Integrating Using the Squared Sine Variant of the Cosine Double-Angle Formula
questions.worked_solution:
Let's recall the double-angle formula for cosine that involves the ${sin}^{2}$ term: 

$$
\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta =1-2{sin}^{2}⁡\theta 
$$

Letting $\theta =\frac{x}{2}$, we have

$$
1-2{sin}^{2}⁡(\frac{x}{2})=\operatorname{cos}⁡x.
$$

Substituting this into our integral, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int (1-2{sin}^{2}⁡(\frac{x}{2}))\text{d}x & =\int \operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡x+C.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.worked_solution:
Here, we use the double-angle formula for cosine that involves the ${cos}^{2}⁡\theta $ term, given by

$$
\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta =2{cos}^{2}⁡\theta -1.
$$

 

Rearranging, we have

$$
{cos}^{2}⁡\theta =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta +1).
$$

Letting $\theta =\frac{x}{2},$ we have

$$
{cos}^{2}⁡(\frac{x}{2})=\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡x+1).
$$

Substituting this into our integral, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {cos}^{2}⁡(\frac{x}{2})\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡x+1)\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\int (\operatorname{cos}⁡x+1)\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{sin}⁡x+x)+C.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14028479/assets/fc3c0c02be98834937150e6bee5a52ac14246bc128b189d3c095269f788d97a9.png)

Find the area $A$ of the region in the $xy$-plane that is bounded by the curve $y=-4{cos}^{2}⁡(2x)+4{sin}^{2}⁡(2x)+{x}^{2}+6,$ the $x$-axis and the lines $x=-\frac{\pi }{4}$ and $x=\frac{\pi }{4},$ as shown above. Do not round the answer.

$A=$
{{field-1}}
questions.worked_solution:
The area of the region is given by

$$
A={\int }_{-\pi /4}^{\pi /4}(-4{cos}^{2}⁡(2x)+4{sin}^{2}⁡(2x)+{x}^{2}+6)\,\text{d}x.
$$

To calculate this integral, we use the double-angle formula for cosine:

$$
\operatorname{cos}⁡2x={cos}^{2}⁡x-{sin}^{2}⁡x
$$

We can rewrite the above formula as

$$
-4\operatorname{cos}⁡4x=-4{cos}^{2}⁡(2x)+4{sin}^{2}⁡(2x).
$$

Hence, the area of the region is

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ={\int }_{-\pi /4}^{\pi /4}(-4{cos}^{2}⁡(2x)+4{sin}^{2}⁡(2x)+{x}^{2}+6)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /4}^{\pi /4}(-4\operatorname{cos}⁡4x+{x}^{2}+6)\,\text{d}x \\  & =(-\operatorname{sin}⁡4x+\frac{{x}^{3}}{3}+6x)\,{|}_{-\pi /4}^{\pi /4} \\  & =[-\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi )+\frac{(\pi /4)^{3}}{3}+6\cdot \frac{\pi }{4}]-[-\operatorname{sin}⁡(-\pi )+\frac{(-\pi /4)^{3}}{3}+6(-\frac{\pi }{4})] \\  & =(0+\frac{{\pi }^{3}}{192}+\frac{3\pi }{2})-(0-\frac{{\pi }^{3}}{192}-\frac{3\pi }{2}) \\  & =\frac{{\pi }^{3}}{96}+3\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14028479/assets/b9a4695c6e43ee5ceb15ea1bbb3ee1815fdbd87e9c8b4a4e8eeba1089750ff79.png)

Find the area $A$ of the region in the $xy$-plane that is bounded by the curve $y=6{cos}^{2}⁡(2x)-6{sin}^{2}⁡(2x)+3x+17,$ the $x$-axis and the lines $x=-\frac{\pi }{2}$ and $x=0,$ as shown above. Do not round the answer.

$A=$
{{field-1}}
questions.worked_solution:
The area of the region is given by

$$
A={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{0}(6{cos}^{2}⁡(2x)-6{sin}^{2}⁡(2x)+3x+17)\,\text{d}x.
$$

To calculate this integral, we use the double-angle formula for cosine:

$$
\operatorname{cos}⁡2x={cos}^{2}⁡x-{sin}^{2}⁡x
$$

We can rewrite the above formula as

$$
6\operatorname{cos}⁡4x=6{cos}^{2}⁡(2x)-6{sin}^{2}⁡(2x).
$$

Hence, the area of the region is

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{0}(6{cos}^{2}⁡(2x)-6{sin}^{2}⁡(2x)+3x+17)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{0}(6\operatorname{cos}⁡4x+3x+17)\,\text{d}x \\  & =(\frac{3}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡4x+\frac{3}{2}{x}^{2}+17x)\,{|}_{-\pi /2}^{0} \\  & =[\frac{3}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(0)+\frac{3}{2}(0)^{2}+17\cdot 0]-[\frac{3}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(-2\pi )+\frac{3}{2}{(-\frac{\pi }{2})}^{2}+17(-\frac{\pi }{2})] \\  & =[0+0+0]-[0+\frac{3{\pi }^{2}}{8}-\frac{17\pi }{2}] \\  & =[0+\frac{17\pi }{2}-\frac{3{\pi }^{2}}{8}]-0 \\  & =\frac{17\pi }{2}-\frac{3{\pi }^{2}}{8}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Integrating Using the Squared Cosine Variant of the Cosine Double-Angle Formula
questions.worked_solution:
Here, we use the double-angle formula for cosine that involves the ${cos}^{2}⁡x$ term, given by

$$
\operatorname{cos}⁡2x=2{cos}^{2}⁡x-1.
$$

 

Rearranging, we have

$$
2{cos}^{2}⁡x=\operatorname{cos}⁡2x+1.
$$

Multiplying both sides by $3,$ we obtain

$$
6{cos}^{2}⁡x=3(\operatorname{cos}⁡2x+1).
$$

Substituting this into our integral, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }6{cos}^{2}⁡x\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }3(\operatorname{cos}⁡2x+1)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={(\frac{3}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡2x+3x)|}_{\pi /2}^{\pi } \\  & =[\frac{3}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\pi )+3\pi ]-[\frac{3}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi )+3\cdot \frac{\pi }{2}] \\  & =3\pi -\frac{3\pi }{2} \\  & =\frac{3\pi }{2}.\end{aligned}
$$
